title: The Art of Setting Deadlines
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article questions the reflexive leadership habit of setting exact, hard deadlines for every task, arguing the practice is often counterproductive because it ignores the uncertainty inherent in real work. It contrasts the short-lived motivational boost of hitting a hard deadline against the corner-cutting and demoralization that follow when deadlines are missed through no real fault of the team. In place of universal hard deadlines, the piece recommends leaders reserve exact deadlines for genuinely do-or-die situations, and default instead to inexact timeframes anchored by clear milestones — arguing that visible incremental progress, not the deadline itself, is what actually sustains team motivation.
points: Exact, hard deadlines are argued to be counterproductive for most tasks because they ignore the genuine uncertainty involved in completing real work.
The piece contrasts the short-lived satisfaction of meeting a hard deadline against the demoralization and corner-cutting that follow repeated, no-fault misses.
The recommended default is inexact deadlines anchored by clear milestones, reserving exact hard deadlines only for genuinely do-or-die situations.
The closing claim reframes what actually motivates teams: not the deadline itself, but the visible momentum of successive milestone achievements.
quotes: Leaders favor exact deadlines to create clarity and accountability.
Because exact deadlines don’t take into account the uncertainties and challenges that may arise during the process, they are often counterproductive.
As the pressure mounts to meet an exact deadline, teams often cut corners and make faulty decisions.
For most projects and tasks, they instead establish inexact deadlines and focus on the milestone goals or steps critical to success.
The best leaders only set exact deadlines when the timing for completion is do or die, or accountability is suspect without it.
The best leaders remember that the ultimate inspiration is not the deadline. It is the forward movement of successive achievements that advance the ball forward.
